# Filtering {background-color="#0C234B"}

## A mask is a Series of booleans

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| min-lines: 9
import pandas as pd

wells = pd.DataFrame({
    "site": ["A-14", "B-07", "C-22", "D-03", "E-11"],
    "depth_ft": [61.0, 1100.0, 835.0, 397.0, 210.0],
    "elev_ft": [2675.0, 2698.0, 2701.0, 2662.0, 2540.0],
})

print(wells["depth_ft"] > 500)
print()
print(wells[wells["depth_ft"] > 500])
```

::: {.fragment}
Exactly last week's numpy mask, with labels along for the ride.
:::

## Combining conditions

```python
deep_and_high = wells[
    (wells["depth_ft"] > 500) & (wells["elev_ft"] > 2680)
]
```

::: {.incremental}
- `&` for and, `|` for or, `~` for not
- **Every condition needs its own parentheses**
- `and` / `or` do *not* work here — they ask for one truth value, and a Series
  has many
:::

::: {.fragment}
Drop the parentheses and `&` binds tighter than `>`, so Python tries
`500 & wells["elev_ft"]` and the error names neither of the things you wrote.
:::

## The silent one

```{pyodide}
#| edit: false
#| autorun: false
#| min-lines: 9
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

s = pd.Series([61.0, np.nan, 835.0])

print(s > 500)          # NaN is neither greater nor less
print()
print(f"rows kept: {(s > 500).sum()} of {len(s)}")
```

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
A comparison against `NaN` is always `False`, so **missing rows are dropped and
never mentioned.** In the real inventory that is 184 wells with no depth on
file. Check `.isna().sum()` before you filter, not after you're confused.
:::

## Your turn: find the shallow northwest wells

Latitude above 32.3, longitude below −111.0, depth under 200 ft.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_filter
import pandas as pd
wells = pd.DataFrame({
    "site": ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"],
    "latitude": [32.35, 32.10, 32.41, 32.38, 32.05],
    "longitude": [-111.05, -110.90, -111.12, -110.85, -111.20],
    "depth_ft": [150.0, 90.0, 180.0, 120.0, 60.0],
})
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_filter
nw_shallow = wells[______]
print(nw_shallow)
print(f"{len(nw_shallow)} wells")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_filter"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

Three conditions joined by `&`, each wrapped in its own parentheses.
:::
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_filter"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2

Longitudes here are negative, so "west of −111.0" means **less than** −111.0.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_filter"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
nw_shallow = wells[
    (wells["latitude"] > 32.3)
    & (wells["longitude"] < -111.0)
    & (wells["depth_ft"] < 200)
]
```

Wells A and C. Well D is far enough north but too far east; E is west enough but
too far south. Negative longitudes reverse the direction your intuition expects,
so say the comparison out loud before you trust it.
:::
:::

# New columns {background-color="#AB0520"}

## Assign to a name that doesn't exist

```python
wells["depth_m"] = wells["depth_ft"] * 0.3048
wells["screen_bottom_elev"] = wells["elev_ft"] - wells["depth_ft"]
```

::: {.fragment}
Elementwise, like numpy. Nothing new — which is the point.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The warning you *will* see:

```
SettingWithCopyWarning: A value is trying to be set on a copy of a slice
```

Take an explicit `.copy()` when you slice a subset you plan to modify. That is
the fix, every time.
:::

## Your turn: decline since the first reading

`depth_to_water_ft` counts **downward**, so a rising number means a falling
water table. Compute how far the level has dropped since the record began.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_newcol
import pandas as pd
one_site = pd.DataFrame({
    "year": [1948, 1965, 1980, 1995, 2010, 2024],
    "depth_to_water_ft": [36.5, 58.2, 101.4, 143.8, 149.1, 147.6],
})
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_newcol
one_site["decline_ft"] = ______
print(one_site)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_newcol"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Subtract the *first* value of the column from the whole column. `.iloc[0]` gets
the first element regardless of what the index labels are.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_newcol"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
one_site["decline_ft"] = (
    one_site["depth_to_water_ft"] - one_site["depth_to_water_ft"].iloc[0]
)
```

111 ft of decline in one well in one lifetime.

These six numbers are made up for the slide. The real well behind them —
D-15-13 11CBA — declined by that much between 1931 and 1994 without turning
around; whether *any* Tucson well has recovered is a question the Week 8 lab
makes you answer from the data rather than take from me.
:::
:::

# Plotting {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Enough to see what you have

```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
ax.plot(one_site["date"], one_site["depth_to_water_ft"])
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_ylabel("depth to water (ft below land surface)")
```

::: {.fragment}
This is the plot you make **while** you're working, not the one you show
people. Week 8 is about the second kind.
:::

## `invert_yaxis()` is not cosmetic

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Without it, depth increases upward, so a **falling water table draws as a rising
line**.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Someone will read that as recovery. In a committee meeting. About your work.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
When the quantity counts downward, so should the axis. This costs one line and
prevents a misreading you cannot take back.
:::

## Your turn: fix the axis

This plots a *falling* water table as a *rising* line. Add the one call that
fixes it, and label the axis so nobody has to guess which way is down.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_plot
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

year = [1948, 1965, 1980, 1995, 2010, 2024]
depth = [36.5, 58.2, 101.4, 143.8, 149.1, 147.6]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
ax.plot(year, depth, color="#AB0520", lw=2, marker="o")
ax.______()
ax.set_ylabel(______)
plt.show()
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_plot"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The method flips the y axis so larger values sit lower. The label needs to say
both the quantity *and* which direction it counts.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_plot"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_ylabel("depth to water (ft below land surface)")
```

`"depth (ft)"` alone would not be enough. Below land surface, or above a datum?
Those differ by about 2,600 ft here, and only the label says which you meant.
:::
:::

## A century, in one well

```{pyodide}
#| edit: false
#| autorun: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.2
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

year = [1948, 1965, 1980, 1995, 2010, 2024]
depth = [36.5, 58.2, 101.4, 143.8, 149.1, 147.6]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(year, depth, color="#AB0520", lw=2, marker="o")
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlabel("year")
ax.set_ylabel("depth to water (ft)")
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.show()
```
